subject: english-language

moments.title: Grice's William James Lectures
moments.body: 1967: Paul Grice delivers the William James Lectures (published 1989 as 'Studies in the Way of Words'). The cooperative principle: 'Make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange.' Four maxims: quantity, quality, relation, manner.
moments.takeaway: Grice's framework explains how we communicate more than we literally say — through 'conversational implicature'.

moments.title: Logic and Conversation
moments.body: 1975: 'Logic and Conversation' is widely published in Cole and Morgan's 'Syntax and Semantics 3'. The four maxims become standard teaching content. Grice's distinction between what is said and what is meant has organised pragmatics ever since.
moments.takeaway: The maxims are not commands but assumptions. Hearers assume speakers are following them and interpret accordingly. Flouting maxims signals implicature.

moments.title: Neo-Gricean and relevance theory
moments.body: Various successors developed Grice's framework. Stephen Levinson's neo-Gricean pragmatics (2000). Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson's Relevance Theory (1986) replaces maxims with a single principle of relevance. Both shape modern pragmatics.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural Gricean studies have shown maxims work differently across cultures — quantity and quality vary; politeness conventions intersect.

now.title: Implicature in everyday life
now.body: Grice's framework is taught at A-level. Modern applications include legal interpretation (what was meant vs said), AI dialogue systems, cross-cultural communication, courtroom evidence. The framework's persistence shows its explanatory power.
now.open_questions: Are Grice's maxims universal? Cultural variation is real but cores of cooperative communication appear robust. The relationship between Gricean assumptions and cultural variation is live in modern pragmatics.

reflection: An Oxford philosopher's analysis of how we communicate meaning beyond literal words organised the modern study of pragmatics. Grice's maxims remain in textbooks 50 years later because the phenomena they describe — implicature, indirect speech — are ubiquitous in human communication.
